Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham
Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham (26 September 1867 – 17 June 1946) was an Indian playwright, novelist and author of short stories, who wrote in the Telugu language.
His father's name is Chilakamarti Venkanna and mother's name is Venkataratnamma and were residents of Veeravasaram village in West Godavari district.
Narasimham's earlier name was Punniah and was later named after a popular temple deity Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy of Antarvedi village.
According to his autobiography, his aunt's daughter Punnamma died after giving birth to a child.
As a boy, he was said to resemble his maternal grandfather, Bhadraiah Sastry who died a year before the grandson was born.
At the age of five, his Upanayanam, the sacred thread ceremony was performed.
His father tried a lot to make Narasimham learn Sandhyavandanam by sending him to his grandfather's village Khandavalli, his aunt's villages Velagadurru and Manchili.
Finally, he stayed in Matsyapuri village near Veeravasaram for several months and learned Trikaala Sandhyavandanam.
But due to the enormity of his service as a social reformer in comparison with that of his work as a pioneer in modern Telugu literature, he is looked upon by the people as a reformer.
The earliest work Keechaka vadha, a stage play, was written in 1889; the last work Bammera Potana, an incomplete play, was written in 1946, the year in which Chilkamarti died.
The works of Chilkamarti can be broadly classified into verses, plays, Prahasanas, novels, long stories and biographies of great men and autobiography.
In 1910, he wrote in Telugu verses, a concise Ramayana of Valmiki.
Chilakamarti is called Andhra Scott after the famous Scottish historical novelist Walter Scott.
Shyamala is another novel written by Chilakamarti based on the Macbeth play of William Shakespeare.

Kandukuri Veeresalingam
Kandukuri Veeresalingam (16 April 1848 – 27 May 1919) was a social reformer and writer from the Madras Presidency, British India, current Andhra Pradesh.
His novel Rajasekhara Charitramu is considered to be the first novel in Telugu literature.
After studying in an Indian street school, he was sent to English medium school where his talent was recognised.

Generally recognised as the first Telugu novel, it is inspired by The Vicar of Wakefield, a novel by the Irish writer Oliver Goldsmith His works include: Rajasekhara Charitramu, first novel in Telugu 'Viveka Vardhini', a journal for women education in 1887. the first drama in Telugu and first book in Telugu on sciences & history.
In 1876, he started a journal called Viveka Vardhini and published articles about women's issues of that area.
The magazine was initially printed in Chennai (then Madras), but with his writings gaining popularity, he set up his own press at Rajahmundry.
Widow remarriage was not appreciated in the society during those days, and he opposed this practice by quoting verses from the Hindu Dharma Sastra to prove his point.
Undeterred, Veeresalingam started a Remarriage Association and sent his students all over Andhra Pradesh to find young single men willing to marry widows.
The Government, in appreciation of his work, conferred on him the title of Rao Bahadur in 1893.
Putali Krishnamurthi, Veeresalingam was probably inspired by the writings of Muddu Narasimham Naidu who pioneered the widow remarriage movement and the rationalist movement in Andhra.
In his memory, the Indian Postal service issued a 25-paisa postage stamp in 1974.

Prabandha
The Prabandha Kosha of Rajashekhara Suri mentions two types of biographical narratives: charitas and prabandhas.
For example, there are texts titled Kumarapala-Charita, Vastupala-Charita and Jagadu-Charita about people who flourished after the end of the 1st millennium CE.
The authors were based in western India, and wrote primarily in colloquial Sanskrit (as opposed to Classical Sanskrit).

Some of the notable Prabandha collections include: Prabandhavali by Jinabhadra, 1234 CE It contains 40 prabandhas about historic personalities (most of them from western India), including Prithviraja Prabandha.
Laghu-Prabandha-Sangraha by anonymous, 13th century It was compiled by a Gujarat-based poet between 1243 CE and 1409 CE.
Prabandha-Chintamani of Merutunga, 1305 CE It contains 135 prabandhas categorized under 11 topics and 5 prakashas (sections).

Vividha-Tirtha-Kalpa or Kalpa-Pradipa by Jinaprabha, 1333 CE 44 of its 63 chapters describes the Jain pilgrimage centres, but it also includes 7 kalpas or chapters covering biographies (that is, prabandhas).
The personalities covered include 10 Suris (Jain teachers), 7 kings, 4 poets, and 3 Jain laymen.
Kumarapala-Prabandha by Jinamandana, 1435 CE Contains 9 prabandhas about Kumarapala, and also provides information about his predecessors and ancestors.
Verses of other poets such as Kalidasa, Subandhu and Magha appear in this collection.
Panchashati-Prabandha-Sambandha by Shubhashila Gani, 1464 CE Contains 625 prabandhas, which are brief accounts of Jain monks and laymen.

Sarangapani
Sarangapani was a composer of Carnatic music who lived during the 17th century in the village of Karvetinagaram in Andhra Pradesh.
His songs were written in tribute to the god Venugoplala, the presiding deity of Venugopalaswamy Temple, Karvetinagaram and contain the mudra "Venugopala".
